values.label: Drug removed after one half-life
values.where: Elimination Half-Life of Drugs, Definition/Introduction: “Although different drugs have varying half-lives, they all share a common principle—after one half-life, 50% of the initial drug amount is removed from the body.”
values.note: The source gives a single value, not a range. The model marker shows how much its drug has lost by the time one usual half-life has passed.

values.label: Drug eliminated after about 3.3 half-lives
values.where: Elimination Half-Life of Drugs, Definition/Introduction: “For example, 90% of a given drug undergoes elimination after approximately 3.3 half-lives.”
values.note: The source gives a single value, not a range. The model marker is read after 3.3 usual half-lives.

values.label: Drug eliminated after 4 to 5 half-lives
values.where: Elimination Half-Life of Drugs, Definition/Introduction: “Moreover, 94% to 97% of a drug is eliminated after 4 to 5 half-lives. Therefore, after 4 to 5 half-lives, the plasma concentration of a given drug typically falls below a clinically relevant concentration and is considered effectively eliminated.”
values.note: The model marker is read halfway through that span, after 4.5 usual half-lives.

values.label: Time to reach steady state, given at regular intervals
values.where: Elimination Half-Life of Drugs, Definition/Introduction: “When administering a drug at regular intervals or a constant amount, such as an infusion, the drug achieves a steady-state concentration after approximately 4 to 5 half-lives” and “This steady state occurs when the drug's infusion rate equals its clearance rate, resulting in a constant net concentration in the body.”
values.note: The model counts steady state as reached once its level stays within one twentieth of its settled level at every point between amounts, including the time absorption takes, and counts the time in usual half-lives. That rule is the model's own choice, not a sourced value.

values.label: Bioavailability of the route in use (reference: intravenous route)
values.where: Drug Bioavailability, Definition/Introduction: “Foundational to how bioavailability is classically defined is that an intravenously administered active drug delivered directly into systemic circulation yields a bioavailability of 100%.” Also Drug Absorption, Clinical Significance: “Drugs administered intravenously (IV) achieve 100% bioavailability because they can directly reach the systemic circulation without the absorption process.”
values.note: Two different things share this row. The black mark is the sourced reference, which is for the intravenous route only and never changes. The blue marker, and the arrows for each state, are the bioavailability of the route the model is using: by mouth at the teaching baseline and for the enzyme and kidney states, by vein for the intravenous state. By mouth it sits below the intravenous reference.

states.label: Enzyme inducers
states.summary: A drug or herb that induces (switches up) the liver's cytochrome P450 enzymes speeds the breakdown of other drugs those enzymes handle, so those drugs are cleared faster and their plasma concentration falls.

evidence.half1: Faster clearance means a shorter half-life, so more is gone by the time one usual half-life has passed. Drug Elimination, Issues of Concern: “The increase in metabolic activity with CYP induction results in a diminished activity of drugs targeted by that particular isoform.” Drug Bioavailability, Definition/Introduction: “Drug clearance can be thought of as the metabolic and excretory factors on the rate and extent an active drug leaves the systemic circulation.” Elimination Half-Life of Drugs, Definition/Introduction: “Equation 3: t1/2=0.693*×Vd*/CL, where Vd is the volume of distribution and CL is clearance.” More metabolic activity raises CL, and a larger CL in Equation 3 gives a shorter half-life.
evidence.ninety: Same reasoning as the row above: Drug Elimination, Issues of Concern: “The increase in metabolic activity with CYP induction results in a diminished activity of drugs targeted by that particular isoform.” With Equation 3, “t1/2=0.693*×Vd*/CL”, a larger clearance shortens the half-life, so more is eliminated by 3.3 usual half-lives.
evidence.effective: Same reasoning: a larger clearance in Equation 3 (“t1/2=0.693*×Vd*/CL, where Vd is the volume of distribution and CL is clearance.”) shortens the half-life, so even more is eliminated by 4.5 usual half-lives.
evidence.steady: Elimination Half-Life of Drugs, Definition/Introduction: “When administering a drug at regular intervals or a constant amount, such as an infusion, the drug achieves a steady-state concentration after approximately 4 to 5 half-lives” With the half-life shortened (Equation 3, larger CL), those 4 to 5 of its own half-lives pass sooner, so counted in usual half-lives steady state comes earlier.
evidence.ivf: Drug Bioavailability, Issues of Concern: “The herbal drug St. John’s wort used most commonly for depression, has been shown to increase cytochrome P450 activity, reducing the plasma concentration, and therefore bioavailability, of other drugs (eg, warfarin) that are also metabolized by cytochrome P450 enzymes.” The arrow is for bioavailability by mouth, the route in use for this state; the intravenous reference value is not changed.

states.where: Drug Elimination, Issues of Concern: “The increase in metabolic activity with CYP induction results in a diminished activity of drugs targeted by that particular isoform.” and “The CYP3A4 is induced by phenytoin, phenobarbital, and St. John's wort, while diltiazem, erythromycin, and grapefruit inhibit it.”
states.modelNote: The model makes the liver clear the drug faster and break down more of it on the first pass. How much faster is an illustrative choice; only the directions come from the source.

states.label: Enzyme inhibitors
states.summary: A drug or food that inhibits the liver's cytochrome P450 enzymes slows the breakdown of other drugs those enzymes handle, so those drugs are cleared more slowly and their plasma concentration rises.

evidence.half1: Slower clearance means a longer half-life, so less is gone by the time one usual half-life has passed. Drug Elimination, Issues of Concern: “Conversely, CYP inhibition will result in increased drug plasma concentration, potentially leading to toxicity.” Drug Bioavailability, Definition/Introduction: “Drug clearance can be thought of as the metabolic and excretory factors on the rate and extent an active drug leaves the systemic circulation.” Elimination Half-Life of Drugs, Clinical Significance, on slowed liver metabolism: “Because the liver inactivates active metabolites at a slower rate, the body requires a longer period to eliminate the drug from circulation.” Equation 3: “t1/2=0.693*×Vd*/CL, where Vd is the volume of distribution and CL is clearance.”
evidence.ninety: Same reasoning as the row above: a smaller clearance in Equation 3 (“t1/2=0.693*×Vd*/CL”) lengthens the half-life, and “the body requires a longer period to eliminate the drug from circulation.” Less is eliminated by 3.3 usual half-lives.
evidence.effective: Same reasoning: with a longer half-life, “the body requires a longer period to eliminate the drug from circulation”, so less is eliminated by 4.5 usual half-lives.
evidence.steady: Elimination Half-Life of Drugs, Definition/Introduction: “When administering a drug at regular intervals or a constant amount, such as an infusion, the drug achieves a steady-state concentration after approximately 4 to 5 half-lives” With the half-life lengthened (Equation 3, smaller CL), those 4 to 5 of its own half-lives take longer, so counted in usual half-lives steady state comes later.
evidence.ivf: Drug Absorption, Issues of Concern: “Before orally administered drugs reach the circulation, they can be metabolized within the gut wall or the liver. This is known as first-pass metabolism, which will decrease the amount of active drug absorbed.” Drug Bioavailability, Issues of Concern: “Notably, hepatic cytochrome P450 metabolism can significantly alter drug bioavailability.” and “Depending on interactions between the unique, temporal portfolio of substances and the target drug, bioavailability may be reduced or enhanced.” Slowed liver enzymes break down less on the first pass, so more of the model's drug taken by mouth reaches the blood; the intravenous reference value itself is not changed.

states.where: Drug Elimination, Issues of Concern: “Conversely, CYP inhibition will result in increased drug plasma concentration, potentially leading to toxicity.” and “The CYP3A4 is induced by phenytoin, phenobarbital, and St. John's wort, while diltiazem, erythromycin, and grapefruit inhibit it.”
states.modelNote: The model makes the liver clear the drug more slowly and break down less of it on the first pass. How much is an illustrative choice; only the directions come from the source.

states.label: Reduced kidney clearance (for example chronic kidney disease)
states.summary: Kidneys that work less well pass less drug into the urine, so a drug the kidneys remove is cleared more slowly, its half-life lengthens and it stays in the blood longer.

evidence.half1: Drug Elimination, Clinical Significance: “Renal disorders, such as chronic kidney disease, can reduce renal function, hindering drug excretion.” Elimination Half-Life of Drugs, Definition/Introduction: “Equation 3: t1/2=0.693*×Vd*/CL, where Vd is the volume of distribution and CL is clearance.” Hindered excretion lowers CL, and a smaller CL in Equation 3 gives a longer half-life, so less is removed by the time one usual half-life has passed.
evidence.ninety: Same reasoning: “Renal disorders, such as chronic kidney disease, can reduce renal function, hindering drug excretion.” With a smaller CL in Equation 3 the half-life is longer, so less is eliminated by 3.3 usual half-lives. Elimination Half-Life of Drugs, Clinical Significance: “In cases of renal failure, drug excretion is impaired”
evidence.effective: Same reasoning: with a smaller CL in Equation 3 (“t1/2=0.693*×Vd*/CL”) the half-life is longer, so less is eliminated by 4.5 usual half-lives. Drug Elimination, Definition/Introduction: “Any significant dysfunction in either organ can result in the accumulation of the drug or its metabolites in toxic concentrations.”
evidence.steady: Elimination Half-Life of Drugs, Definition/Introduction: “When administering a drug at regular intervals or a constant amount, such as an infusion, the drug achieves a steady-state concentration after approximately 4 to 5 half-lives” With the half-life lengthened (Equation 3, smaller CL), those 4 to 5 of its own half-lives take longer, so counted in usual half-lives steady state comes later.
evidence.ivf: Not stated. Drug Bioavailability, Definition/Introduction, says: “Any degree of failure to eliminate a drug may augment its bioavailability by maintaining a larger drug plasma concentration than would normally be expected over time.” That describes the level kept up over time, not the share that reaches the blood, which is what this row and the model measure (“For most purposes, bioavailability is defined as the fraction of the active form of a drug that reaches systemic circulation unaltered.”). No change in that share is stated, so no arrow is shown and the model holds it.

states.where: Drug Elimination, Clinical Significance: “Renal disorders, such as chronic kidney disease, can reduce renal function, hindering drug excretion.” Together with Elimination Half-Life of Drugs, Definition/Introduction: “Equation 3: t1/2=0.693*×Vd*/CL, where Vd is the volume of distribution and CL is clearance.”
states.modelNote: The model's drug is removed half by the liver and half by the kidneys; here the kidney share is cut. How much is an illustrative choice; only the directions come from the source.

states.label: Intravenous route (compared with by mouth)
states.summary: Given straight into a vein, the drug reaches the blood at once and whole: it skips absorption from the gut and the liver's first-pass metabolism.

evidence.half1: Unchanged. Elimination Half-Life of Drugs, Definition/Introduction: “Equation 3: t1/2=0.693*×Vd*/CL, where Vd is the volume of distribution and CL is clearance.” The route is not in the equation, so the half-life does not change with it.
evidence.ninety: Unchanged. The half-life does not depend on the route (Equation 3: “t1/2=0.693*×Vd*/CL”), and the chapter says “certain quantitative constants apply to all drugs exhibiting first-order pharmacokinetics.”
evidence.effective: Unchanged, for the same reason: “certain quantitative constants apply to all drugs exhibiting first-order pharmacokinetics.” and the half-life (Equation 3) has no term for the route.
evidence.steady: Unchanged. “When administering a drug at regular intervals or a constant amount, such as an infusion, the drug achieves a steady-state concentration after approximately 4 to 5 half-lives” The time is counted in half-lives, and the half-life (Equation 3) does not change with the route.
evidence.ivf: Drug Absorption, Clinical Significance: “Drugs administered intravenously (IV) achieve 100% bioavailability because they can directly reach the systemic circulation without the absorption process.” Drug Bioavailability, Definition/Introduction: “On the contrary, an intravenous (IV) drug is assumed to be immediately delivered to the systemic circulation because it is not subject to absorption or first-pass metabolism”

states.where: Drug Bioavailability, Definition/Introduction: “On the contrary, an intravenous (IV) drug is assumed to be immediately delivered to the systemic circulation because it is not subject to absorption or first-pass metabolism” and Drug Elimination, Issues of Concern: “Intravenously administered drugs are not subject to the first-pass effect.”
states.modelNote: The model gives the same amount, at the same times, straight into the blood instead of by mouth. Removal is unchanged.
